title: Floor-IT: Information-Theoretic BFT in Partial Synchrony with Two Round Good Case Latency and Optimal Resilience
authors: Ittai Abraham, Yuval Efron, Jovan Komatovic, and Alejandro Ranchal-Pedrosa
abstract: In the information-theoretic model, parties communicate over sender-authenticated point-to-point channels, but use no digital signatures or other transferable cryptographic certificates; the adversary is otherwise computationally unbounded. We present \name, an information-theoretic Byzantine agreement protocol for partial synchrony with a good-case latency of two rounds that achieves the optimal resilience bound of $n = 5f - 1$ in this setting. When the actual network delay after GST is at most $\delta \le \Delta$, our protocol achieves a \emph{robust} good-case latency of $2\delta$. The protocol proceeds in views and guarantees a worst-case view latency of at most $2\Delta + 2\delta$. Moreover, each party requires only $O(1)$ words of persistent storage, and each view incurs $O(n^2)$ messages of $O(1)$ words each.

In the information-theoretic model, parties communicate over sender-authenticated point-to-point channels,
but use no digital signatures or other transferable cryptographic certificates; the adversary is otherwise
computationally unbounded. We present Floor-IT, an information-theoretic Byzantine agreement protocol
for partial synchrony with a good-case latency of two rounds that achieves the optimal resilience bound of
𝑛 = 5𝑓 − 1 in this setting. When the actual network delay after GST is at most 𝛿 ≤ Δ, our protocol achieves a
robust good-case latency of 2𝛿. The protocol proceeds in views and guarantees a worst-case view latency of
at most 2Δ + 2𝛿. Moreover, each party requires only 𝑂 (1) words of persistent storage, and each view incurs
𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) messages of 𝑂 (1) words each.

1   Introduction
In the Byzantine agreement problem, 𝑛 processes, of which up to 𝑓 may be corrupted and behave
arbitrarily, must decide on a common value [52]. The problem remains central to fault-tolerant
computing, underlying both blockchain finality and replicated services. Most deployed protocols
assume partial synchrony [37]: the network behaves asynchronously until an unknown Global
Stabilization Time (GST), after which every message arrives within a known bound Δ; the unknown
actual bound on message delays is denoted by 𝛿 ≤ Δ. They are also typically leader-based: execution
is divided into numbered views, each with a designated leader that proposes a value while the other
processes vote.
Good-case latency and worst-case view length. Beyond correctness, a practical consensus
protocol must decide quickly when conditions are favorable and recover quickly from views that
do not decide. In partial synchrony, these requirements are captured by two latency measures.
Decision latency is measured from GST. Good-case latency considers executions in which GST is
zero and the first leader is correct. Its robust variant, robust good-case latency, considers executions
in which GST coincides with a correct leader entering a view, provided no correct process has
previously entered that view or any higher view. View length measures how long it can take all
correct processes to move past a post-GST view, once every correct process has reached that view
or a higher one. Together, the two measures bound decision time after GST and the delay that
faulty leaders can impose.
   With transferable signatures, both measures are well understood. PBFT [31] decides in three
rounds, 3𝛿, at the optimal resilience 𝑛 = 3𝑓 + 1, and three rounds is optimal at that resilience [13].
Tendermint [22] reduced the per-view communication from 𝑂 (𝑛 3 ) to 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) while storing only
𝑂 (1) state, and Simplex [24] reduced the view length to 3Δ + 𝛿. Reducing the good-case latency
below 3𝛿 requires more processes per fault. FaB Paxos [54] achieves two-round, 2𝛿, decisions with
𝑛 = 5𝑓 + 1 processes; subsequent work established the tight threshold: two-round decisions are
achievable if and only if 𝑛 ≥ 5𝑓 − 1 [13, 50].
   Without transferable signatures, fewer matching bounds were known. In the signature-free,
information-theoretic (IT) setting, point-to-point channels identify the sender, but the adversary
reads every message and is computationally unbounded. No process can forward a transferable

the relevant messages. This setting avoids trusted setup and cryptographic computation, and its
guarantees are unaffected by future cryptanalytic advances, including quantum attacks. For years,
the best known IT protocols were slower than their authenticated counterparts. IT-HotStuff [17]
and TetraBFT [64] identified closing this gap as an open problem. TetraBFT achieved a good-case
latency of 5𝛿 with constant storage, while leaving the optimal good-case latency in this setting open.
Forget-IT [4] resolved this question: at the optimal resilience 𝑛 = 3𝑓 + 1, it achieves the optimal
good-case latency of 3𝛿, with 𝑂 (1) words of persistent storage, 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) messages per view, a view
length of 7Δ, and optimistic responsiveness. Fast TetraBFT [40] subsequently matched the optimal
3𝛿 by adding a fast path to TetraBFT’s first view. Thus, at 𝑛 = 3𝑓 + 1, transferable cryptography
does not improve the optimal good-case latency.
   DGV gave a two-step execution without authentication, but its recovery uses signed view-change
proofs [36]. The 𝑛 = 5𝑓 − 1 constructions in [12, 13, 50] also use transferable signatures. A recent
chained construction is signature-free end to end [6], but does not establish 𝑂 (1) persistent storage.
These results leave open the following question:
         Does there exist an information-theoretic BFT protocol that decides in two rounds, at
         the optimal two-round resilience of 𝑛 = 5𝑓 − 1, with 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) messages of 𝑂 (1) words
         each per view and 𝑂 (1) persistent storage?
Main result. We answer this question affirmatively with Floor-IT, a deterministic Byzantine agree-
ment protocol that tolerates a full-information, computationally unbounded adversary corrupting
𝑓 ≥ 2 of 𝑛 = 5𝑓 − 1 processes, while storing only 𝑂 (1) words of persistent memory. After GST,
when the leader is correct, Floor-IT decides in two rounds: one message delay for voting and one for
deciding, so every correct process decides within 2𝛿 of the proposal. Thus, neither the two-round
decision procedure nor view change and recovery requires transferable cryptography. The result
refutes a conjecture of Abraham et al. [13] that two-round signature-free Byzantine broadcast
under partial synchrony requires 𝑛 ≥ 5𝑓 + 1.1
Theorem 1 (Informal). For every 𝑓 ≥ 2, there exists a deterministic, information-theoretic Byzantine
agreement protocol on 𝑛 = 5𝑓 − 1 processes that is optimistically responsive, achieves good-case and
robust good-case latencies of 2𝛿, has a view length of 2Δ + 2𝛿, uses 𝑂 (1) words of persistent storage,
and sends 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) messages per view.

Related Work
Byzantine agreement. Introduced by Lamport, Shostak, and Pease [52, 57], Byzantine agreement
asks 𝑛 processes, up to 𝑓 of which may fail arbitrarily, to converge on a common value; the problem
has since grown a literature far too broad to survey here [2, 7, 23, 27, 28, 30, 42, 45, 51, 55, 60, 61, 63].
The FLP impossibility [41] rules out deterministic solutions under full asynchrony; determinism is
recovered under synchrony [33] and under partial synchrony [31, 37], the model of this paper.
Latency of Byzantine agreement. The yardstick by which agreement protocols are most com-
monly measured is latency: the number of message delays until every correct process decides.
Under synchrony, the Dolev–Strong protocol [33] solves broadcast in 𝑓 + 1 rounds, which is
worst-case optimal, while early-stopping protocols [32] terminate within 𝑓 ′ + 2 rounds when
only 𝑓 ′ < 𝑓 faults actually occur. Under asynchrony, Bracha’s reliable broadcast [21] completes

Good-case latency. The study of the happy path opens with PBFT [31] and its good-case latency

presented that resilience as necessary. The claimed lower bound is not a general 5𝑓 + 1 lower
bound: it applies to the restricted architecture in which proposer and acceptor roles are disjoint [50].
Without that restriction, Kuznetsov, Tonkikh, and Zhang [50] and Abraham et al. [13] established
the tight 𝑛 = 5𝑓 − 1 boundary for two-round authenticated broadcast and co-located BFT replicas,
alongside the optimality of 3𝛿 at 𝑛 = 3𝑓 + 1. This issue is separate from the protocol itself: a
later audit found a liveness flaw in the original Parameterized FaB view change (and a safety flaw
in Zyzzyva), and subsequent work gave repaired fast/slow view changes [10, 11, 44]. In parallel,
Tendermint [22] demonstrated that PBFT’s latency is compatible with 𝑂 (1) storage and 𝑂 (𝑛 2 )
communication per view, and, following [13], the good-case landscape has been charted along
many further axes [9, 14, 16, 19, 38].
The unauthenticated setting. Closest to our work are the unauthenticated protocols that share
our concern for persistent storage; Table 2 juxtaposes them against Floor-IT. IT-HotStuff [17] and
TetraBFT [64] both combine 𝑂 (1) persistent memory with 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) messages per view and optimistic
responsiveness, reaching good-case latencies of 6𝛿 and 5𝛿, respectively, and Forget-IT [4] settled
the question at optimal resilience, pairing the optimal (robust) good-case latency of 3𝛿 with the
same storage and communication guarantees. The very recent Fast TetraBFT [40] then matched the
optimal 3𝛿 with a simpler design, a fast-path wrapper around TetraBFT confined to the first view;
as the fast path never returns after view 0, the robust variant remains that of the base protocol.
An early result comes close to this setting. For Algorithm 1 of Dutta, Guerraoui, and Vukolić [36],
constellation 𝐶 2 requires 𝑁𝑎 > max{2(𝑀 −1) +𝐹 +2𝑄, 2𝑀 +𝐹 +𝑄 } acceptors. Setting 𝑀 = 𝑄 = 𝐹 = 𝑓
gives 𝑁𝑎 ≥ 5𝑓 − 1 for 𝑓 ≥ 2 (and 𝑁𝑎 ≥ 5 for 𝑓 = 1). Its favorable two-round execution needs no
authentication, but the complete algorithm uses signed view-change messages and signed view
proofs; it is therefore not an end-to-end signature-free protocol. Moreover, 𝑁𝑎 is an acceptor count
and becomes the replica count only when the roles are co-located. Floor-IT removes signatures
from both the fast path and recovery: it delivers 2𝛿 at 𝑛 = 5𝑓 − 1 while retaining 𝑂 (1) persistent
storage, 𝑂 (𝑛 2 ) logical communication per view, and responsiveness.

Roadmap
We introduce the system model and formally state the problem in §2. Then, in §3, we present
Floor-IT, laying out its pseudocode and walking through the ideas that drive it. Finally, in §4, we
establish Floor-IT’s correctness and complexity in full detail.

2   Preliminaries

Processes & the adversary. Our system comprises a static set {𝑝 1, 𝑝 2, . . . , 𝑝𝑛 } of 𝑛 = 5𝑓 − 1
message-passing processes, for some integer 𝑓 ≥ 2. Every process is modeled as a deterministic
state machine that possesses a local clock. During an execution, an adversary can corrupt as many as
𝑓 processes, at any point in time; an adversary with this power is said to be 𝑓 -bounded. A corrupted
process is Byzantine and can deviate arbitrarily from the protocol, whereas a non-corrupted process
behaves exactly as its state machine prescribes; the former processes are called faulty, and the latter
correct. Additionally, the adversary is assumed to be (1) full-information, i.e., it has access to the
internal state of every process, and (2) computationally unbounded. Lastly, since local computation
is negligible relative to message delays, we treat it as instantaneous.

Communication network. Processes communicate over a point-to-point message-passing net-
work with authenticated channels: the recipient of a message can verify who sent it. Reliability,
however, is not among our assumptions. Following prior work that shares our concern for constant
persistent storage [5, 34], we adopt an unreliable network in which all communication unfolds
through broadcasts: a broadcast operation unicasts the message to every process individually and
retransmits it, again and again, until the operation is explicitly abandoned, following the semantics
of [34]. Within this model, a message 𝑚 is alive at time 𝜏 if its broadcast has been initiated, but not
abandoned, by time 𝜏; it is forever-alive if its broadcast, once initiated, is never abandoned.

the model introduced in [5]: the state machine of every process contains a designated persistent
memory component along with rules that specify how this component evolves over time. Namely,
beyond Byzantine corruptions, the adversary can also temporarily crash correct processes, under

the guarantee that each crashed correct process eventually recovers. A crashed process sends
no messages and performs no local computation; in particular, every broadcasting operation it
initiated prior to crashing is implicitly abandoned. Crucially, however, the crash leaves the process’s
persistent memory intact. Moreover, handlers execute atomically with respect to crashes: a crash
may strike only between handler executions.2 Once it recovers, the process runs a designated
recovery procedure—a purely local computation whose sole input is the contents of persistent
memory, with access to no other information, neither volatile state nor messages received in the
past. This procedure yields a new local state, from which the process continues executing its state
machine as normal; timers resume from their persisted values. Finally, so that reasoning about
sub-linear (in 𝑛) storage is meaningful, the identities of the participating processes are assumed
to reside in a read-only part of the state machine that remains resilient to crashes and whose size
does not count towards the process’s persistent memory.
Partial synchrony. We adopt the standard partially synchronous model [37]. In this model, an
unknown Global Stabilization Time (GST), selected by the adversary, splits the execution into
an initial asynchronous period followed by a synchronous one. During the synchronous period,
message delays are bounded by a known constant Δ: every message broadcast at time 𝜏 that remains
alive throughout [𝜏, max(𝜏, GST) + Δ] is received by time max(𝜏, GST) + Δ. Furthermore, we write

   Additionally, every correct process is assumed to start executing the protocol no later than GST,
and hardware clocks, though they may drift arbitrarily before GST, exhibit no drift afterwards.
Finally, the adversary is allowed to crash correct processes only prior to GST, and each crashed
correct process is guaranteed to also recover before GST. Consequently, all correct processes are
continuously online from GST onward.
Byzantine agreement & its metrics. This work designs a Byzantine agreement protocol operating
in the model described above. Formally, we address the problem where each correct process proposes
an initial value and seeks to decide a value such that the following properties are satisfied:
      • Agreement: Correct processes never decide different values.
      • Termination: Each correct process eventually decides.
      • Non-triviality: If GST = 0, all processes are correct, and all propose the same value 𝑣, then
        no correct process decides a value other than 𝑣.
Although various other validity constraints exist [29], we intentionally adopt the simplest formula-
tion so as to keep the focus on the core algorithmic challenges, which do not depend on the specific
validity variant.
Efficiency metrics. Three key metrics underpin our evaluation of protocol efficiency. Given an
𝑓 -bounded adversary A (capable of corrupting up to 𝑓 processes) and an 𝑓 -secure (resilient to
𝑓 corrupted processes) leader-based Byzantine agreement protocol Π, let DL A (Π) denote the
smallest time 𝑇 by which, in the presence of A, every correct process decides (but not necessarily
terminates), normalized to GST, i.e., DL A (Π) = 𝑇 − GST(A). (Here, GST(A) denotes the GST of a
given adversary A.) Given a family F of 𝑓 -bounded adversaries, the decision latency of Π with
respect to F is defined as DL F (Π) = sup A ∈ F DL A (Π).
      • Good-case latency Tgc : Let Fgc denote the family of 𝑓 -bounded adversaries A under which
        GST = 0 and the first leader ℓ is correct. We define Tgc ≜ DL Fgc (Π).
      • Robust good-case latency Trgc : Let Frgc denote the family of 𝑓 -bounded adversaries A under
        which GST coincides with a correct leader entering its view, no correct process having
        entered that view or any greater view beforehand. We define Trgc ≜ DL Frgc (Π).
      • Memory complexity PM(Π): Under an adversary A, let PM A (𝑝𝑖 , 𝜏) denote the size (in words)
        of the persistent memory register of a correct process 𝑝𝑖 at time 𝜏, where a single word
        can hold a constant number of messages, values, and counters. The memory complexity
        of Π with respect to A is then PM A (Π) = maxcorrect 𝑝𝑖 ,𝜏 ∈N PM A (𝑝𝑖 , 𝜏), while the overall
        memory complexity of Π is PM(Π) = max 𝑓 -bounded A PM A (Π).
